messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Kofi's Story

Kofi was sixty-eight when the car hit him. He had been a dancer since he was twelve years old—first in Accra, then in London, finally in New York, where he had spent forty years teaching modern dance at a studio in Brooklyn and performing in community productions. His wife, Ama, had died three years earlier, and dancing had become even more essential to him; it was the language in which he still felt fluent, the one place where his body did not betray him. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, he was crossing Atlantic Avenue after buying groceries, the sun warm on his shoulders, thinking about the evening class he was about to teach. A delivery truck ran a red light. The impact came from his left side, a sound he could not now describe and a sensation of his ribs compressing, the world tilting, the pavement rushing toward his face.

He spent four days in the hospital. The doctors said he was fortunate—no internal bleeding, no fractures, significant bruising and soft tissue trauma but nothing that would not heal. What they did not say, and what Kofi came to believe with absolute certainty, was that his body had been fundamentally compromised. In the weeks after discharge, when he tried to return to teaching, his movements felt foreign to him, as though he were operating a machine he no longer understood. His knees buckled unexpectedly. His balance, which had been perfect for fifty-six years, now felt precarious. He could no longer trust his own body to do what he commanded it to do. This distrust extended into every corner of his life. If his body could fail him so catastrophically on an ordinary afternoon, how could he trust his judgment about anything else? He began to doubt whether he was making the right decisions, whether his perceptions of situations were sound. He could not trust that he would do the right thing anymore.

The memories of the collision itself were fragmented and incomplete. Kofi could recall the sun and the grocery bags—one had split, apples rolling across the street—but the moment of impact remained opaque, as though a section of film had been cut out. When he tried deliberately to reconstruct what had happened, to piece together a coherent story, the effort felt like pushing against a locked door. His mind would seize up. The harder he tried to remember, the more the fragments scattered. He would lie awake at night attempting to assemble a narrative of those seconds, but the gaps terrified him more than the fragments did. Not knowing what he had not seen, what he had missed, what might have happened in those missing moments—it made him feel vulnerable in a way he could not articulate. Because the memory was so fractured and incomplete, he found himself unable to predict danger. If he could not remember what had happened, how could he protect himself from it happening again? The fragmentation of his memory seemed to confirm his deepest fear: that the world was fundamentally unpredictable and that he was powerless within it.

This fear manifested as an acute hypervigilance that governed every moment outside his apartment. Kofi felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the room. In his kitchen, he repositioned himself constantly, turning to face the window, then the doorway, then back again. When he went to the grocery store—and he went as infrequently as possible now—he would stand with his cart against a shelf, scanning the aisles, his shoulders rigid. He was on high alert when he heard unexpected or loud sounds; a car horn from the street below would send a jolt through his chest. When something took longer than expected, he assumed something bad was happening. A delayed text from his daughter made him certain she had been in an accident. A longer-than-usual wait at the pharmacy meant the pharmacist had discovered something wrong with his prescription, some institutional failure that would harm him. These interpretations felt less like thoughts and more like facts, immediate and undeniable.

The threat he felt everywhere made it impossible to go out. What had once been a simple errand—walking to the bodega, catching the bus to the studio—became a gauntlet of danger. He began to avoid going out altogether, or when he did venture out, he moved quickly and rigidly, his jaw clenched, his mind cataloguing exits. He stopped answering calls from friends and former students. Seeing people he had socialized with before the event became intolerable; they would ask how he was, and he could not bear to explain, could not find the words for how fundamentally altered he was. So he avoided them. He also avoided thinking about anything discussed in therapy—the accident itself, the specifics of his fears—because engaging with those thoughts felt like stepping into the path of the truck all over again. His world contracted week by week. He stopped teaching. He stopped going to the studio. He stopped going out except for the bare necessities, and even those trips left him trembling and exhausted.

Kofi came to see his therapist because his daughter had insisted, threatening to move back in with him if he did not get help. What frightened him most now was not the memory of the collision itself—that remained mercifully inaccessible—but the possibility that he would spend the rest of his life imprisoned by his own vigilance, his body a cage, his mind a locked room where the truth of what happened would never be fully recovered. He was sixty-eight years old and had lost the only language he had ever truly spoken.
